item.title: What If AI Stopped Talking? Inside Jev, System One Models, and RLCD
item.content:encoded:
LLMs are great at generating text. But many software systems do not need generated text.

They need decisions.

For example:

  • Is this transaction suspicious?
  • Which team should handle this ticket?
  • Is this RAG document relevant?
  • Should this incident be escalated?
  • How severe is this failure?

Today, we often use a generative LLM for these tasks.

That usually looks like this:

It works.

But it is a surprisingly heavy pipeline for something that may ultimately be a classification problem.

TypeSafe AI is proposing a different approach with Jev, the first model in what it calls System One Models.

Instead of generating text, Jev directly returns typed probabilistic decisions.

The Core Idea

A System One model behaves more like:

state → decision distribution

rather than:

prompt → generated text

Conceptually:

The model handles fuzzy judgment.

Your application keeps control.

That separation is important.

Why “System One”?

The terminology is inspired by Daniel Kahneman’s System 1 and System 2 distinction.

System 1 represents fast judgment.

System 2 represents slower, deliberate reasoning.

For AI systems:

Does this message contain PII?

is closer to a System One task.

But:

Investigate this outage,
find the root cause,
compare three solutions,
and recommend a migration strategy.

requires deeper reasoning.

Jev is focused on the first category.

It is not trying to replace reasoning models.

Where Jev Fits

A useful mental model is:

Use code when the logic is obvious.

if amount > 5000:
    require_approval()

Use a decision model when the rule is semantic.

Does this transaction look suspicious?

Use a reasoning model when the task requires investigation or planning.

Investigate why fraud increased this month.

How Modern LLM Training Usually Works

Before understanding RLCD, it helps to understand the typical LLM pipeline.

Each technique optimises for a different outcome.

Step 1: Pretraining

A language model starts with a simple objective:

Predict the next token.

For tokens:

x₁, x₂, ... xₙ

the model learns:

P(xₜ | x₁, x₂ ... xₜ₋₁)

The training objective is roughly:

L = -Σ log P(xₜ | previous tokens)

After enough data and compute, sophisticated capabilities emerge.

But pretraining does not directly optimize for:

  • helpfulness
  • instruction following
  • honesty
  • calibrated confidence

That requires post-training.

Step 2: Supervised Fine-Tuning

Humans provide examples of good responses.

This teaches the model how useful assistant responses should look.

But multiple responses can still be valid.

Which one is better?

That’s where RLHF comes in.

RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

RLHF optimizes models based on human preference.

A simplified flow:

Humans might say:

B > A > C

A reward model learns to approximate those preferences.

The language model is then optimized to receive higher reward.

In simple terms:

Pretraining:
What token is likely next?
RLHF:
What answer would humans prefer?

RLHF is excellent for conversational AI.

But there is a catch.

Human preference is not the same thing as probability calibration.

A confident-sounding answer can still be wrong.

RLVR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

Some tasks have objectively checkable answers.

For example:

  • mathematics
  • coding
  • theorem proving
  • structured reasoning

Instead of asking a human whether an answer looks good, we can verify it automatically.

For coding:

Generate code
     ↓
Run tests
     ↓
Pass / Fail
     ↓
Reward

RLVR is powerful because the reward is based on correctness rather than preference.

But many production decisions cannot be verified instantly.

Consider:

Will this customer churn?
Is this ticket urgent?
Should this incident be escalated?
Is this document relevant?

These tasks need another property:

good uncertainty estimates.

RLCD: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions

TypeSafe calls its approach:

Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.

The goal is not just to output a decision.

It is to output a probability that reflects how reliable that decision is.

Example:

P(escalation required) = 0.92

This is where calibration matters.

What Is Calibration?

Suppose a model makes 1,000 predictions with probability:

0.80

If the model is well calibrated, roughly:

800 / 1000

should actually be correct.

Formally:

P(Y = 1 | predicted probability = p) ≈ p

For example:

Prediction confidence: 0.9
Expected real correctness: ~90%

This property is very useful for automation.

Accuracy Is Not Calibration

Consider two models.

Model A

Accuracy: 92%
Confidence:
Almost always 99%

Model B

Accuracy: 90%
0.95 predictions → ~95% correct
0.80 predictions → ~80% correct
0.60 predictions → ~60% correct

Model A has slightly higher raw accuracy.

But Model B may be easier to use safely in automation.

Your system can implement:

if probability >= 0.95:
    automate()
elif probability >= 0.75:
    verify()
else:
    human_review()

Now confidence becomes part of the application architecture.

RLHF vs RLVR vs RLCD

The simplest comparison is:

Or visually:

These approaches solve different problems.

Jev’s Three Core Primitives

Jev currently exposes three main decision types.

1. Choice

Use Choice when one predefined option must be selected.

Example:

Which team owns this incident?
application
infrastructure
database
data_pipeline

Possible output:

{
  "choice": "infrastructure",
  "probabilities": {
    "application": 0.04,
    "infrastructure": 0.84,
    "database": 0.03,
    "data_pipeline": 0.09
  }
}

This is useful for:

  • intent classification
  • ticket routing
  • tool selection
  • document categorization
  • workflow routing

2. Score

Score represents an ordered scale.

For example:

How severe is this incident?
0 → Informational
1 → Minor
2 → Moderate
3 → Major
4 → Critical

Instead of simply returning:

3

the model can produce a distribution across the scale.

This works well for:

  • severity
  • quality
  • risk
  • relevance
  • urgency

3. Noul

Noul represents the probability that a proposition is true.

Example:

Does this incident require escalation?

Output:

0.94

This means:

P(escalation = true) = 0.94

It does not mean:

The incident is 94% severe.

For severity, Score is more appropriate.

One State, Multiple Decisions

The useful part is that multiple questions can be asked about the same state.

The model provides decisions.

Code owns the workflow.

Why This Could Be Faster

Traditional LLM generation is autoregressive.

Each generated token depends on previous output.

Jev does not need to generate long arbitrary sequences.

Its output space is constrained.

That allows a very different inference pattern.

TypeSafe says Jev questions can be evaluated in parallel.

That is one reason this model class can potentially have much lower latency than a generative workflow.

Does Jev Really Have “Zero Hallucinations”?

This claim needs nuance.

Suppose a Choice supports:

billing
technical
sales

Jev cannot suddenly produce:

finance

It also avoids several common generative failure modes:

  • malformed JSON
  • unsupported enum values
  • unexpected prose
  • invented schema fields

That is valuable.

But Jev can still select:

technical

when the correct answer was:

billing

So the more accurate distinction is:

Jev removes generation failures. It does not remove incorrect predictions.

How I Would Use It in an Agent System

The most interesting architecture is not:

Jev Instead of LLM

It is:

That creates a clean separation:

LLM ---> Reason and generate.
Jev ---> Judge and score.
Code ---> Control and execute.

This feels much more production-friendly than giving an agent unrestricted control.

Jev in a RAG Pipeline

Jev also fits naturally into RAG evaluation.

A normal pipeline:

A decision model could be inserted after retrieval:

You could ask:

Does this document help answer the query?

and filter documents based on probability.

It could also evaluate the final response:

Is this answer supported by the retrieved context?
Does it fully answer the question?
Does it contradict the evidence?

That could make Jev interesting as an AI evaluator.

How I Would Benchmark It

Do not test this with five Playground examples.

Use a real dataset.

Something like:

I would measure:

  • accuracy
  • precision
  • recall
  • F1
  • Brier score
  • Expected Calibration Error
  • p50 latency
  • p95 latency
  • p99 latency
  • cost per 1,000 decisions
  • repeated-run stability

But I would add one more metric:

accuracy at different confidence thresholds.

Confidence-Gated Automation

Suppose your results look like this:

Now you can make an engineering decision.

For example:

At confidence >= 0.90,
we can automate roughly half of requests
at approximately 99% observed accuracy.

That is far more useful than simply saying:

The model achieved 92% accuracy.

Where Jev Makes Sense

Jev is not a general-purpose replacement for an LLM.

It is a specialized decision primitive.

The Bigger Architectural Shift

Most AI applications today start with:

What prompt should I write?

System One models encourage a better question:

What decision does my software actually need?

That leads to a cleaner architecture.

Instead of treating AI as a giant autonomous worker, we start treating different models as specialized software primitives.

Final Thought

RLHF taught models:

What answer will humans prefer?

RLVR asks:

Can this answer be objectively verified?

RLCD asks something different:

What decision should I make,
and how confident should I actually be?

That distinction is what makes Jev interesting.

The future AI stack may not be:

One giant model doing everything.

It may look more like:

Or even more simply:

Reasoning models → think.
Decision models → judge.
Software → acts.

Whether Jev and RLCD deliver on that promise still needs independent benchmarking.

But the architectural idea is worth paying attention to.

item.title: Bribing the Bouncer: What the Hell is a Preflight Request?
item.content:encoded:
Bribing the Bouncer: What the Hell is a Preflight Request?

Every web developer remembers their rite of passage. You spin up a backend service, write a shiny client-side script, fire off a simple fetch() or axios.post() call, and lean back to admire your craftsmanship.

Then your browser console explodes in vibrant, radioactive red:

“Access to fetch at ‘https://api.backend.com' from origin ‘https://this-is-my-app.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn’t pass access control check…

You pop open the DevTools Network tab expecting to troubleshoot your payload, only to find an uninvited guest masquerading as an HTTP method: OPTIONS.

You never wrote an OPTIONS request. Nobody writes OPTIONS requests on purpose. So who invited it, and why is it sabotaging your sprint?

Welcome to the browser’s favorite surveillance mechanism: The Preflight Request.

The VIP Lounge Analogy

Think of the web ecosystem as a slightly pretentious, high-end night club:

  • Your Client Code: A wide-eyed clubber eager to get in and dance with the database.
  • The API Server: The exclusive venue with an intimidating dress code.
  • The Browser: Your ridiculously overprotective parent who drove you to the club and refuses to let you out of the car until they speak with the manager.

If you roll up wearing plain clothes — like submitting an old-school HTML form or firing a basic GET query—the browser shrugs and lets you go. The W3C calls this a Simple Request. The risk is minimal, and the server knows how to handle common foot traffic.

Then modern single-page apps happened. Now you walk up to the door and tell your browser:

  1. “I’m carrying a fancy leather briefcase.” (Content-Type: application/json)
  2. “I’ve got an exclusive backstage pass pinned to my lapel.” (Authorization: Bearer <token>)
  3. “Also, I plan on ripping out a VIP booth and putting a new one in.” (PUT, PATCH, or DELETE)

At that point, the browser grabs you by the collar: “Hold your horses, rockstar. You can’t just storm in dressed like an enterprise payload. Let me check with the bouncer first to see if they tolerate your existence.”

That recon scout dispatched by the browser is the Preflight Request.

The Walkie-Talkie Wiretap

If you listen in on the network traffic right before your code actually executes, the negotiation looks remarkably bureaucratic.

The Browser asks permission via OPTIONS:

HTTP

OPTIONS /api/v1/checkout HTTP/1.1
Host: api.backend.com
Origin: https://this-is-my-app.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization

Subtext: “Hey bouncer. Kid from https://this-is-my-app.com wants to send a POST. They want to bring JSON and an Authorization header. Are we cool, or are you calling security?"

If the backend engineer configured CORS properly, the server nods and waves the green flag:

The Server responds (usually with a 204 No Content or 200 OK):

HTTP

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://this-is-my-app.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST, GET, OPTIONS, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400

Subtext: “Yeah, we know that domain. They can run a POST, and those headers are fine. Also, write this down: don't ask me again for the next 24 hours (86400 seconds)."

Once the browser hears that, it finally lets go of your sleeve and fires your actual, intended POST request.

Two Landmines That Break Prod

Preflight isn’t malicious; it exists to shield legacy endpoints from unauthorized cross-origin mutations. Still, it trips up even experienced teams in two hilarious ways:

1. The Overzealous JWT Guard

You build a global authentication middleware that intercepts every incoming request to verify bearer tokens.

Here’s the catch: Preflight OPTIONS requests do not carry user credentials.

Your server promptly smacks the OPTIONS call with a 401 Unauthorized. The browser concludes the bouncer threw a punch, so it kills your real request before it ever leaves the station.

Fix: Exempt OPTIONS methods from your auth guards. Never demand an ID from the messenger asking where the door is.

2. Network Latency Ping-Pong

If you trigger a preflight check before every single API mutation, you double your round-trip time. On spotty cellular connections, your slick single-page app suddenly feels like dial-up.

Fix: Set a healthy Access-Control-Max-Age header on preflight responses. Tell the browser to cache the verdict so it doesn't run back to the bouncer every two seconds.

Preflight requests aren’t a bug in your code; they are the browser running security clearance behind your back. The next time the console paints your screen red, don’t scream at your framework — just check the OPTIONS exchange to see which header offended the bouncer.

item.title: Is Bitcoin Ready for Q-Day?
item.content:encoded:
Why Is Everyone Talking About Q-Day?

Quantum computers are getting better at solving problems that today’s cryptography relies on. If they become powerful enough, they could eventually break some of the cryptographic systems protecting Bitcoin, online banking, digital signatures, and much more.

That point in time is often called Q-Day.

It hasn’t happened yet, and today’s quantum computers are nowhere near powerful enough to break Bitcoin’s cryptography. But the possibility is serious enough that Bitcoin developers are already discussing how the network could transition to quantum-resistant cryptography, including proposals such as BIP-360.

How Bitcoin Stores Money (UTXO Model)

Bitcoin doesn’t track one account balance the way a bank does. Instead, your Bitcoin exists as separate pieces of value called UTXOs (Unspent Transaction Outputs), which remain unspent until you use them.

Think cash, not a bank balance. A $4 balance in a bank account is one number, but $4 in your pocket might be made up of a few separate bills or coins.

When you send Bitcoin, your wallet doesn’t simply “deduct” the amount. It selects existing UTXOs as inputs, spends them completely, and creates new UTXOs as outputs, including any change sent back to you. The old UTXOs are spent and can no longer be used.

This is why Bitcoin is better understood as a collection of independently locked pieces of value rather than a single account balance.

There’s no central “wallet balance” anywhere on the network.

How a Crypto Address Actually Locks and Unlocks Bitcoin

When someone sends Bitcoin to you, they don’t send it directly to your name or wallet. Instead, the Bitcoin is locked by a spending condition that determines what you need to prove before you can spend it.

For common address types such as P2PKH and P2WPKH, that condition is based on a hash of the recipient’s public key.

Step 1: Alex Locks the Bitcoin (Sending to Julia)

When Alex sends BTC to Julia, he doesn’t send it directly to “Julia.” He sends it to an address that represents a spending condition based on her public key.

e.g.

Lock condition:
Hash(public key) must match Julia's address

At this point, the blockchain only needs the hash. Julia’s actual public key isn’t revealed until she spends the Bitcoin.

Step 2: Julia Spends It

When Julia wants to send this BTC to someone else, the network needs proof that she is allowed to spend it.

Her wallet creates a new transaction and provides,

1. Her real public key   → so nodes can check: Hash(public key) == address
2. A brand-new signature → proves she approved THIS transaction

Step 3: Every Validator Verifies the Transaction

There is no single trusted checker. Nodes across the network independently verify the transaction.

For this type of address, they can check:

Does the public key match the address? (Hash(public key) == wallet address) ✅
Is the signature valid for this transaction?  ✅

The first check connects Julia’s public key to the Bitcoin being spent. The second proves that she authorized the transaction with the corresponding private key.

Because every node needs to verify the transaction independently, Julia’s public key is included in the transaction she broadcasts. It isn’t something she can reveal only to selected validators.

Step 4: The Public Key Is Now Public

Once Julia spends the Bitcoin, her public key is recorded in the transaction on the blockchain.

From that point on, anyone can see it. It remains publicly available as part of Bitcoin’s permanent transaction history.

The Real Vulnerability

Now that we’ve seen how Bitcoin locks and unlocks coins, here’s the actual security question behind Q-Day; what part of this process could a quantum computer actually attack?

What Is NOT at Risk

For common address types such as P2PKH and P2WPKH, the blockchain initially stores a hash of the public key, not the public key itself.

A hash can’t simply be reversed to reveal the public key behind it. As long as the coins remain behind an address that has never been spent from, the public key remains hidden.

Hashed public key → not directly exposed to a quantum attack

What IS at Risk

The situation changes once the public key is revealed.

For P2PKH and P2WPKH, this normally happens when the coins are spent. The public key is then included in the transaction and permanently recorded on the blockchain.

Some other output types, such as P2PK and P2TR, expose a public key as part of the output itself, so their exposure happens earlier.

Exposed public key → vulnerable to future quantum key recovery

Why “Vulnerable” Doesn’t Mean “Instantly Hacked”

An exposed public key isn’t cracked the second it appears. Recovering the private key would still require a quantum computer powerful enough to run Shor’s algorithm hardware that doesn’t exist yet.

Exposed public key ≠ stolen coins
Exposed public key = a future opportunity for an attack

Why This Still Matters Today

The problem is that once a public key is exposed, it can never be made private again.

An attacker could potentially collect exposed public keys today and target them once sufficiently powerful quantum hardware exists.

This is why some Bitcoin holdings are already more exposed than others. Very old addresses that have already been spent from, as well as address types where the public key is visible from the beginning, have already exposed their keys.

Nobody Agrees on the Timeline

So when will a quantum computer actually become powerful enough to do this? Nobody knows.

The exact timeline is impossible to know today. What matters is that Bitcoin needs to prepare before sufficiently powerful quantum hardware exists.

Quantum Risk in Bitcoin Today

Not all Bitcoin is exposed to quantum attacks in the same way. There are two different attack windows.

1. Short-Range Attack

When it happens: After you broadcast a transaction but before it is confirmed.

Window size: ~10 minutes (average time for the next block).

How it would work: A quantum attacker would see your exposed public key in the mempool, derive the private key, and broadcast a competing transaction before your original transaction is confirmed.

Reality check: This requires a quantum computer fast enough to break ECDSA in minutes. Estimates suggest cryptographically relevant quantum computers may not emerge until the 2030s or later, with some analyses projecting 10–20 years — and even then, doing it in under 10 minutes is a much higher requirement than doing it at all.

https://coinshares.com/corp/insights/research-data/quantum-vulnerability-in-bitcoin-a-manageable-risk

2. Long-Range Attack

When it happens: any time after a public key has ever been exposed on-chain — from an old spend, address reuse, or certain address types.

Window size: unlimited. Attackers can collect exposed public keys today and simply wait.

How it would work: An attacker could collect exposed public keys and wait until quantum hardware becomes powerful enough to recover the corresponding private keys. Project Eleven

Reality check: Researchers expect attackers to prioritize this method there’s more vulnerable Bitcoin to target, a higher chance of success, and less chance of being noticed compared to a mempool race.

How Much Bitcoin Is Actually at Risk Right Now?

There are several estimates of how much Bitcoin has already exposed its public key. The numbers vary depending on how “at risk” is defined and which address types are included.

  • Satoshi-era P2PK addresses~1.7 million BTC BeInCrypto where the public key is exposed directly, from day one.
  • Reused / spent-from addresses ~25%-35% of total BTC supply Onramp BitcoinPublic key revealed once spent, and still sits at that address
  • Long-range vulnerable total~4.49 million BTC (~$495B) Human Rights FoundationCan still be moved to safety before quantum computers catch up

Public Key Exposure

Building on what we covered earlier — a locking script only stores a hash of your public key, and spending is what reveals the real key — here’s how that plays out differently across every address type Bitcoin has used.

The simple pattern underneath all of this

Hash-based locks (P2PKH, P2WPKH, P2SH, P2WSH)
   → SAFE while unspent
   → EXPOSED only after you spend
   → Fix: never reuse the address

Public-key-based locks (P2PK, P2TR)
   → EXPOSED the moment you receive
   → Fix: eventually migrate to post-quantum address types

Solutions & Proposed Fixes

What You Can Do Right Now

Even before any protocol changes go live, there’s already a simple mitigation available today:

Never reuse a Bitcoin address. Once you spend from an address, its public key is permanently exposed. Move funds to a fresh address afterward, and be cautious about parking large balances on already-exposed addresses (spent-from legacy addresses, or Taproot addresses in general).

This doesn’t fix the underlying cryptography — it just avoids leaving coins sitting behind a key that’s already out in the open.

What Bitcoin Itself Is Proposing

Two proposals are currently working through Bitcoin’s improvement process — one for the future, one for the past.

BIP-360

BIP-360’s immediate fix is narrow: it solves Taproot’s specific problem — the public key being exposed the moment you receive funds, not just when you spend. Its new address type, P2MR (bc1z...), removes that exposed key-path entirely, so nothing but a hash is visible until you spend.

But BIP-360 is really two things happening at once:

  1. What it fixes today: Taproot’s early-exposure flaw — one specific, narrow problem
  2. What it prepares for tomorrow: a framework that can carry and verify real quantum-resistant signature algorithms, once those are ready

Right now, BIP-360 doesn’t yet include actual post-quantum math — it’s building the container, not the contents. A future BIP will plug real quantum-resistant signature schemes (like Dilithium or FALCON) into this same framework.

Status
Draft. BIP-360 has been published in the Bitcoin BIPs repository, but it has not been activated on Bitcoin mainnet. Bitcoin/BIPS

BIP-361

BIP-361 tackles a different problem than BIP-360. Where BIP-360 fixes Taproot’s exposure issue for future transactions, BIP-361 (Post Quantum Migration and Legacy Signature Sunset) deals with coins that are already exposed today — old, dormant addresses whose public keys are already sitting on-chain.

The Core Idea

Problem: ~6.5-6.9 million BTC already sit in addresses with exposed public keys
         Many are dormant — owners lost their keys, or it's Satoshi-era coins
         These can never be "moved to safety" voluntarily.

BIP-361's proposal: set a deadline. Coins not migrated to quantum-safe 
                     addresses by a certain point could become unspendable.

What This Means Practically

  • If your coins sit behind an exposed public key, BIP-361 would give you a window to move them to a new, safer address type.
  • If you don’t move them in time, the protocol itself could make them permanently frozen/unspendable — a “use it or lose it” ultimatum.

Why It’s Controversial

This directly clashes with one of Bitcoin’s core principles; no one — not even the community via consensus — should be able to seize or destroy someone else’s coins. Freezing dormant coins (including likely Satoshi holdings) protects the network from a future quantum thief scooping them up, but permanently locks out any legitimate owner who’s simply lost access, alive or not.

Status
Published in 2026, BIP-361 is still a draft proposal. It is one approach to the “Burn vs. Steal vs. Hourglass” debate we discussed earlier, proposing a phased transition away from quantum-vulnerable outputs rather than leaving the problem unresolved. Bitcoin/BIPS

Why Quantum Computers Can’t Break This Yet

Breaking Bitcoin’s encryption needs quantum computers built from logical qubits — a stable, reliable, error-free version of a qubit, made by combining many physical qubits together to correct each other’s mistakes. Regular physical qubits alone are too noisy and unreliable to trust for something this important.

Today’s best quantum computers have only around a thousand physical qubits and out of those, only a tiny handful actually work reliably enough to count as true logical qubits. Breaking Bitcoin is estimated to need over a thousand logical qubits, working perfectly, at once.

The gap between “what we have” and “what’s needed” is still huge — which is exactly why Bitcoin isn’t breakable today.

Conclusion

If Q-Day arrived unprepared, it wouldn’t just threaten Bitcoin — it could shake trust in the digital infrastructure the world now runs on. But just as the world quietly solved Y2K before it became a crisis, Bitcoin still has time to shift toward quantum-resistant cryptography before Q-Day ever arrives.
